gaps.sentence: All candidates must ___ the written exam in June.
gaps.hint: collocation with 'exam' from the candidate's side
gaps.explanation: take an exam (or sit an exam) means to be tested; 'give an exam' is not used in British English.

gaps.sentence: We ___ our shopping at the local market every Saturday.
gaps.explanation: do the shopping is the collocation for buying food and household goods.

gaps.sentence: I only ___ sight of the celebrity for a second before the crowd closed in.
gaps.explanation: catch sight of somebody/something means to notice them briefly.

gaps.sentence: The roads were almost empty — the traffic was surprisingly ___.
gaps.explanation: light traffic means few vehicles on the road; its opposite is heavy traffic.

gaps.sentence: Make sure you are fully ___ of the terms before you sign.
gaps.explanation: fully aware of something is the fixed collocation meaning knowing completely.

gaps.sentence: It's your turn to ___ care of the dog this weekend.
gaps.explanation: take care of somebody/something means to look after them.

gaps.sentence: He ___ her a compliment on her new hairstyle.
gaps.explanation: pay somebody a compliment is the fixed collocation for praising someone.

gaps.sentence: Our guide was highly ___ and had climbed the mountain five times.
gaps.explanation: highly experienced is the standard collocation; 'highly' combines with participial adjectives.
